📖 Core Definitions

Essential Terminology & Concepts

Permutation Core Definition

Permutation the random rearrangement of elements in a sequence.

Discretisation And Binning Key Concept

Discretisation is the process of converting continuous numeric data into discrete categories to facilitate certain modelling techniques.

Conceptual Framework: Why Discretise? Key Concept

This process is called Discretisation or Binning.

Method 2: Equal-Frequency Binning Key Concept

pd.qcut() Equal-Frequency Binning, implemented using pd.qcut(), focuses on balancing the number of observations in each bin, rather than balancing the range.

Detecting And Filtering Outliers Key Concept

Outliers are data points that deviate significantly from other observations.

📌 Key Takeaways

Section-by-Section Study Breakdown

3.2 Discretisation and Binning

  • Discretisation is the process of converting continuous numeric data into discrete categories to facilitate certain modelling techniques.
  • This section describes the process in detail.
  • This process is called Discretisation or Binning.
  • For example, instead of using the exact Monthly_Salary (e.g., 50000, 68000, 150000), we may prefer to categorise it into 'Low Salary', 'Medium Salary', and 'High Salary'.

3.2.1 Conceptual Framework: Why Discretise?

  • This process is called Discretisation or Binning.
  • For example, instead of using the exact Monthly_Salary (e.g., 50000, 68000, 150000), we may prefer to categorise it into 'Low Salary', 'Medium Salary', and 'High Salary'.
  • We may group ‘Age’ into 5 or 10 age ranges (e.g., 0-10, 11-20, etc.).
  • This process offers several benefits: • Data Simplification: By grouping values, we reduce the complexity of the dataset and make it easier to analyse and interpret.

3.2.2 Method 1: Equal-Width Binning with pd.cut()

  • In Equal-Width Binning, the range of the variable (calculated as Maximum value minus Minimum value) is divided into a predetermined number of intervals (N), where each interval has the exact same width.
  • For example, if marks range from 40 to 100 (range of 60), and we choose N=4 bins, each bin will have a width of 15 (60/4).
  • We use the Pandas function pd.cut() for this method.
  • Let us try an example using the above dataset.

3.2.3 Method 2: Equal-Frequency Binning

  • pd.qcut() Equal-Frequency Binning, implemented using pd.qcut(), focuses on balancing the number of observations in each bin, rather than balancing the range.
  • This method uses percentiles, or quantiles, to define the bin boundaries.
  • For instance, if we request four bins (quartiles), the boundaries will be defined such that the 25th, 50th, 75th, and 100th percentiles split the data, resulting in approximately equal counts in each bin.
  • This approach is particularly valuable when the underlying data distribution is highly skewed, preventing all or most data points from clustering into one or two large bins.

3.2.4 Comparison of pd.cut() and pd.qcut()

  • Let us look at the fundamental difference between these two powerful discretization tools: Function Basis of Division Focus/Criteria Best Used When...
  • pd.cut() Equal Value Range (Equal Width) The distance between the bin edges must be equal.
  • Domain knowledge dictates fixed ranges (e.g., age groups, scores out of 100).
  • pd.qcut() Equal Observation Count (Equal Frequency) The number of data points in each bin must be equal (or nearly equal).

3.3 Detecting and Filtering Outliers

  • Outliers are data points that deviate significantly from other observations.
  • They represent rare occurrences, measurement errors, or genuine extreme values.
  • If ignored, outliers can skew statistical averages (like the mean) and standard deviations, potentially leading to poorly generalised analytical models.
  • Effective data transformation requires robust methods for detecting and managing these anomalies.

3.3.1 Visualisation: Identifying Outliers with Box Plots

  • The essential first step in outlier management is visualisation.
  • The Box Plot (or Box- and-Whisker Plot) is the standard tool for quickly identifying data spread and potential outliers.
  • It provides a clear graphical representation, showing the median and quartiles.
  • Please note it uses seaborn library of Python, which is used for making the box plot on Annual Income.

3.3.2 Method Selection: Z-score versus IQR

  • The choice of numerical detection method depends critically on the underlying data distribution.
  • Z-Score Method The Z-score method assumes that the data is normally (Gaussian) distributed.
  • It measures how many standard deviations a data point deviates from the mean.
  • Outliers are typically defined as values with a Z-score greater than a threshold, commonly ±2 or ±3.
